title: Progress: dashboards, burn charts, exceptions and OKRs
blurb: Report progress with the right dashboard or report, read burn charts and flow diagrams, spot an exception and use OKRs and maturity assessments.
question: Draycott's board is used to monthly written reports. How should it see progress between stage boundaries in PRINCE2 Agile, and what should happen if a burn chart shows a Must have will be missed?

teach.body: The progress practice compares what has been achieved with what was planned, forecasts whether objectives can still be met and controls deviations that would cause an exception. In agile, time and cost have zero tolerance, so tracking them against tolerance tells you little. Flexibility in what is delivered is the aspect that matters most, which is why burn charts suit every level. Control uses metrics checked regularly, such as Kanban lead time, and informal, visual reporting through workshops, burn charts and dashboards.

teach.body: An exception occurs when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. An updated burn chart at iteration or release level may be the trigger; hold an immediate meeting on the options before escalating to the board in an exception report. OKRs set aspirational objectives with specific, measurable key results; teams define or update them in the release planning workshop. Agile maturity assessments track psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1, 12.3.2.3, 12.4.1, Table 13.16

steps.label: Exception report
steps.sub: To the board, with a recommendation

teach.body: The board is used to monthly written reports, so project manager Andrea Lucas sets up a project dashboard in the kickoff workshop with the release status, a burn-up of machines connected and current risks; board members pull from it and review it at each progress review. The software team keeps its own team dashboard. In Release 2 the burn-up shows prediction alerts, a Must have, will miss month 8, so Andrea meets the team on options at once and sends the board an exception report.

teach.text: Traps: the team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report and the project dashboard replaces the highlight and end stage reports, not the other way round. Burn-down = work left, team level; burn-up = work completed, project level; a CFD shows workflow states. An exception is a forecast breach of tolerance, reported in an exception report, not a highlight report. The PM attends stand-ups only with the team's agreement.

items: What is delivered is the aspect to watch; time and cost have zero tolerance.
Team dashboard = checkpoint report; project dashboard = highlight and end stage reports.
Burn-down (team, work left), burn-up (project, work done), CFD (bottlenecks).
Forecast breach of tolerance: immediate meeting on options, then an exception report.
OKRs in the release planning workshop; maturity assessments track safety, maturity, sustainability.

summary: You can now choose the right dashboard, log or report for a progress need and read burn-down, burn-up and cumulative flow charts. You can also recognize when a forecast creates an exception and apply OKRs and agile maturity assessments in a scenario.

A.q: Easterholm County Council's assistant director wants regular progress information between stage boundaries. The project manager proposes a project dashboard, updated in each progress review workshop, which board members can look at whenever they wish. Which PRINCE2 management product does this replace?
A.why: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report (and the end stage report); it is updated in progress review workshops and the board pulls information from it (Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: The checkpoint report is replaced by the team dashboard, which the PM pulls from.
whyNot.2: An exception report is still produced when a plan is forecast to exceed tolerance; the dashboard does not replace it.
whyNot.3: The end project report reviews performance against the PID at closure, not regular progress.

A.q: Halfway through a sprint, Larkspur Rail's app team looks at its burn-down chart. The actual line is well above the ideal line. What does this show, and what should the team do?
options: It is ahead, so it can pull in extra stories
It is on track, so no action is needed
It is behind, so it should add a week to the sprint
It is behind, so it should focus on top priorities
A.why: Actual above ideal on a burn-down means not enough work is being done; the team will not complete everything at this rate and should focus on the highest-priority items (12.4.3).

whyNot.0: Above the ideal line on a burn-down means more work is left than planned, so the team is behind.
whyNot.1: A gap above the ideal line means the team is behind, which needs attention.
whyNot.2: Timeboxes are fixed; time does not flex, so the team adjusts what is delivered instead.

A.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's board wants to see, across stages and iterations, how much of the click and collect product has been completed against the Easter deadline, and to forecast when the work will be finished. Which chart suits this BEST?
A.why: A burn-up chart shows completed work against a deadline at project or product level, over stages or iterations, to forecast completion (12.4.3).

whyNot.1: A burn-down shows outstanding work over time, usually at team level within an iteration.
whyNot.2: A cumulative flow diagram shows items in each workflow state to reveal bottlenecks, mostly at team level.
whyNot.3: A cumulative risk burn-down tracks total risk exposure, not completed work.

B.q: Pinewick's store operations team uses Kanban to move each store through preparation, training and go-live. It wants a chart showing how many stores sit in each state over time, so it can see where work is piling up. Which technique should it use?
options: A burn-up chart of stores live
A release map of store waves
B.why: A cumulative flow diagram shows tasks in each workflow state over time and helps identify bottlenecks (12.4.2).

whyNot.0: A burn-up shows completed work against a deadline, not how many items are in each state.
whyNot.1: A release map plans releases and features; it does not show workflow states over time.
whyNot.3: A team skill matrix maps capabilities and gaps, not the flow of work.

B.q: In Saltmarsh Housing Group's release planning workshop at the end of stage 2, the service design team sets itself the goal 'make the first visit the only visit' with measurable results such as 'second visits below 20% by month 8'. Which progress artifact is the team creating?
B.why: OKRs combine clear, aspirational objectives with specific, measurable key results; teams define or update them in the release planning workshop at stage boundaries (12.3.2.3, Table 13.16).

whyNot.0: A Definition of Done sets criteria for completing work items, not team goals with measurable results.
whyNot.2: The release map is updated in the same workshop, but it plans releases and features rather than setting goals.
whyNot.3: The project canvas sets out the business justification for the project as a whole.

B.q: Callowmere University's agile coach measures psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability across the teams at each stage, to track how well the new ways of working are taking hold. Which progress technique is this?
B.why: Agile maturity assessments are a progress technique whose key metrics include psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability (12.4.1).

whyNot.0: The Agilometer is a risk tool assessing the risks of agile working, not these maturity metrics.
whyNot.1: A cumulative flow diagram shows work in each workflow state over time.
whyNot.2: A burn-up chart shows completed work against a deadline.

C.q: Draycott's project manager, Andrea Lucas, wants first-hand progress information, so she starts attending the software team's daily stand-ups without asking the team. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
options: Yes, because she needs progress for the project dashboard
Yes, because the PM pulls information from the team
No, because she may attend with the team's agreement
No, because stand-ups are run by the product owner
C.why: The project manager may attend daily stand-ups with the delivery team's agreement; she cannot decide to attend on her own (Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: She does need progress information, but she can pull it from the team dashboard rather than join stand-ups uninvited.
whyNot.1: The PM pulls information from the team dashboard; that does not give her the right to attend stand-ups unasked.
whyNot.3: Who facilitates the stand-up is not the point; attendance by the PM needs the team's agreement.

C.q: Larkspur Rail's finance director wants monthly spend against budget to be the main measure of progress. The project manager proposes burn charts of features delivered as the main measure instead, because time and cost have zero tolerance. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
options: Yes, because what is delivered is the aspect that flexes
Yes, because burn charts replace the business case
No, because spend should be the main progress measure
No, because burn charts belong at team level
C.why: With zero tolerance on time and cost, flexibility in what is delivered is the primary aspect of interest, so burn charts are used at every level (12.3.1).

whyNot.1: Burn charts track progress; the business case, as the project canvas, still justifies the project.
whyNot.2: Tracking spend against a zero-tolerance budget tells the board little; what is delivered is what flexes.
whyNot.3: Burn-downs are usually team level, but burn-ups are used at project and product level.

C.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's updated Release 2 burn-up forecasts that the engineer parts list, a Must have, will not be delivered by month 8, which is outside tolerance. Project manager Sally Greaves calls an immediate meeting with the team leads to examine the options, then sends an exception report to the board. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
options: Yes, because options are explored, then the board is told
Yes, because forecasts are covered by highlight reports
No, because the team should extend the release date
No, because the board is told at the end of the stage
C.why: An exception may be triggered by an updated burn chart; the guidance is an immediate meeting on the options before escalating to the board with an exception report (Table 12.1).

whyNot.1: Highlight reporting gives regular status; a forecast breach of tolerance needs an exception report.
whyNot.2: Time has zero tolerance; extending the date is not the team's to decide and breaks the fixed timebox.
whyNot.3: Waiting for the stage end would leave the board unaware of a forecast breach of tolerance.

reteach.title: Training for a marathon
reteach.question: A runner has a fixed race date. How does she know if her training is on track, and when should she tell her coach something is wrong?

blocks.body: Her weekly plan shows miles left to run this week: if the line stays above the target, she is behind and does the key sessions first. A season chart shows total miles banked against race day. Her coach looks at her training app whenever she likes, rather than waiting for a written report. If an injury means she cannot reach the minimum long run before race day, she talks options through straight away, then tells the coach with a recommendation.

head: Marathon
PRINCE2 Agile
rows: Coach checks the app any time
Project dashboard, pulled by the board
Injury puts the minimum at risk

blocks.text: Moving the race is not an option: the date is fixed. What flexes is how much training she fits in.

explain.body: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report and is updated in team planning and retrospectives; the PM pulls from it. The project dashboard replaces the highlight and end stage reports and is updated in progress reviews; the board pulls from it.

test.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's project manager wants to know how the service design team's iteration is going without asking for a written checkpoint report. What should she use?
test.why: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report; it is updated in team workshops and the PM extracts information as needed (Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: The project dashboard is the board's view of the whole project, replacing the highlight report.
whyNot.2: The end stage report, replaced by the project dashboard, reviews a whole stage for the board.
whyNot.3: The lessons report shares lessons; it does not show an iteration's progress.

explain.body: Burn-down: work left, usually team level, days in an iteration. Burn-up: completed work against a deadline, project level. Cumulative flow diagram: items in each workflow state, to spot bottlenecks.

root.label: What do you need to know?

test.q: Callowmere University's web team wants a chart of the story points still outstanding on each day of its current two-week sprint. Which chart should it use?
test.why: A burn-down chart shows outstanding work over time, often story points over the days of an iteration at team level (12.4.3).

whyNot.0: A burn-up shows completed work against a deadline, usually at project or product level.
whyNot.1: A cumulative flow diagram shows items in each workflow state, not points left.
whyNot.3: A cumulative risk burn-down tracks total risk exposure, not work.

explain.body: An exception exists when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, for example when an updated burn chart shows a Must have will not be delivered in time. Explore the options at once, then send an exception report to the board.

test.q: Easterholm County Council's burn-up for Release 1 now forecasts that the carers' self-assessment, the minimum the council must deliver, will not be ready by the release deadline. This is outside the tolerance the board set. Which report should go to the board?
test.why: When a stage or project plan is forecast to exceed tolerance, the PM informs the board with an exception report giving options and a recommendation (Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: A lessons report shares lessons; it does not escalate a forecast breach of tolerance.
whyNot.1: The end stage report (project dashboard) reviews a completed stage, not a forecast breach.
whyNot.2: An issue report analyses one issue's impact and options; a plan forecast to exceed tolerance needs an exception report.

explain.body: The digital and data management approach says how data and information will be created, used, managed and kept secure. The daily log is the PM's informal diary from starting up; the lessons log keeps lessons for this and future projects.

test.q: Draycott's project dashboard will draw live sensor data from all 60 machines, and the union has asked how worker data will be protected. Where should the project set out how this data will be created, used, stored and kept secure?
options: The digital and data management approach
test.why: The digital and data management approach describes how data and information will be created, used and managed through the project and afterwards, including security and privacy (Table 12.1; PRINCE2 7 management products).

whyNot.0: The daily log is the PM's informal diary, not the place for data management rules.
whyNot.2: The communication management approach covers communication with stakeholders, not data handling and security.
whyNot.3: The team dashboard displays a team's progress; it does not define how data is managed.
